ABSTRACT: Confinement of hydrocarbons in nanoscale pockets and pores provides tunable capability for controlling molecules in catalysts, sorbents, and membranes for reaction and separation applications. While computation of the enthalpic interactions of hydrocarbons in confined spaces has improved, understanding and predicting the entropy of confined molecules remains a challenge. Here we show, using a set of nine aluminosilicate zeolite frameworks with broad variation in pore and cavity structure, that the entropy of adsorption can be predicted as a linear combination of rotational and translational entropy. The extent of entropy lost upon adsorption is predicted using only a single material descriptor, the occupiable volume ( $ V_{occ} $). Predictive capability of confined molecular entropy permits an understanding of the relation with adsorption enthalpy, the ability to computationally screen microporous materials, and an understanding of the role of confinement on the kinetics of molecules in confined spaces.

On the basis of this shape-selective feature , highly effective molecular separations and selective catalytic conversions can be achieved within zeolitic structures that are difficult to accomplish with other materials and/or techniques . $ ^ { 1-3 } $ So far, several shape-selectivity mechanisms have been elucidated and applications identified. $ ^{2-18} $ In common molecular sieving, bulky molecules adsorb preferentially over bulkier species as a result of steric constraints imposed by the zeolites' framework, e.g., linear alkane molecules compared to branched isomers. $ ^{19-23} $ Besides this common adsorption competition based on molecular bulkiness, the reverse phenomenon can also occur, i.e., competitive adsorption in favor of the bulkier species. The enthalpy and the entropy contributions to the Gibbs free energies were calculated at T = 298 K and partial pressure of 1 atm (101325 Pa). The enthalpy (H) of gas-phase pyridine and acetonitrile molecules is defined as the sum of total electronic energy ( $ E_{el} $), internal vibrational energy ( $ E_{v} $), zero-point vibrational energy (ZPVE), as well as the rotational and translational contributions to the internal energy: $ H = E_{el} + E_{v} + ZPVE + E_{R} + E_{t} $. The corresponding calculated entropies (S) includes translational, ( $ S_{t} $) vibrational, ( $ S_{v} $) and rotational ( $ S_{r} $) degrees of freedom: $ S = S_{t} + S_{v} + S_{r} $. All the considered systems are in singlet state, thus the electronic contribution to the entropy is zero. Since both adsorbed molecules are constrained in the zeolite cavity their entropy contributions in the adsorption complexes were corrected as follows: the translational and rotational degrees of freedom were reduced by 1 and 1.28 [37]. 1.2.1. Framework dynamics. The first attempts to describe guest-induced flexibility in zeolites were done using molecular dynamics simulations. $ ^{79-82} $ Rigid zeolitic force fields were dynamically modified using transition state theory to include lattice flexibility, and the results obtained by these models were in good agreement with experimental data. $ ^{79-81,83,84} $ It was shown that framework flexibility in silicalite-1 (MFI-type framework) is responsible for the adsorption of large molecules such as isobutane and heptane with inflection behavior at high loadings, $ ^{80} $ while enhanced self-diffusivity at low loadings of short alkanes (i.e. methane and n-butane) was observed. $ ^{81} $ Framework flexibility is also crucial for aromatics adsorption on MFI zeolite, especially at high pressures. $ ^{84,85} $ While the use of rigid zeolitic models led to the underestimation of the aromatics adsorption in MFI zeolite by a factor of two, $ ^{84,85} $ the use of flexible models to simulate diffusion coefficients of various alkanes in silicalite-1 zeolite resulted in a convergence of experimental and theoretical values. $ ^{86} $ Recently by using in situ integrated differential phase contrast scanning transmission electron microscopy (iDPC-STEM) while adsorbing benzene molecules on MFI zeolite, Xiong et al. showed that the MFI structure goes through severe deformations giving another proof of guest-induced flexibility in zeolites (see Fig. 4). $ ^{87} $

2.4.4. Trapdoor. Traditional diﬀusion models primarily consider two types of interactions: those between guest molecules (guest–guest) and those between guest molecules and the zeolite framework (guest–host). However, when cations are present in the zeolite structure, a third interaction—involving guest molecules, the framework, and cations (guest–host-cation)—must also be accounted for. A striking example of such ternary interactions is the well-known ‘‘molecular trapdoor’’. This phenomenon, also referred to as the ‘‘gating effect’’, describes a unique molecular sieving mechanism in certain zeolites and related porous materi- als. Here, extra-framework cations function as dynamic gate- keepers at pore apertures, selectively controlling molecular diffusion to achieve highly discriminative adsorption and separation.9,147,187 To date, ‘‘trapdoor’’ has been observed in several zeolites, including RHO (DNL-6),188–190 CHA (SAPO-34, SSZ-13),147,191,192 MWF (ZSM-25),149,193 HEU (Clinoptilolite),194

descriptor_candidates.name: occ_volume_confinement_ratio
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss (s_gas - s_ads)/R correlates with the ratio of framework accessible volume per gram to molecular van der Waals volume; tighter ratio means stronger confinement and larger entropy loss. Adding this nonlinear re-expression on top of the full 14-input network lowers MAE of entropy loss/R versus the baseline network.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E01/E03: entropy loss upon adsorption is governed by confinement, and occupiable volume is the dominant single descriptor. Normalizing accessible pore volume (AV, cm^3/g) by molecular volume (Vol, angstrom^3) proxies how tightly the guest packs per unit pore space, coupling molecular size and framework void.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If the MAE of (s_gas - s_ads)/R does not decrease relative to the 14-input baseline when this descriptor is ablated or emphasized, or if the descriptor's partial dependence is flat/monotone in the wrong direction, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: shape_asymmetry_pmi
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Molecular rotatability under confinement depends on the anisotropy of the inertia tensor: near-spherical or highly anisotropic molecules lose entropy differently than intermediate-asymmetry tops. Incorporating this normalized PMI shape factor reduces MAE of entropy loss/R beyond baseline.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E01/E06: adsorbed entropy is decomposed into translational and rotational parts; rotational freezing is controlled by the moments of inertia (PMI1-3). A dimensionless anisotropy index captures how many rotational modes are quenched by pore walls, distinct from size alone.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If the partial dependence of entropy loss/R on this shape factor shows no statistically distinguishable structure (e.g., permutation test p > 0.05) or MAE does not improve, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: aperture_span_mismatch
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss peaks when the pore-limiting diameter (lsd_p) closely matches the molecule's span (SPAN): near-equal sizes lock the molecule in place (max entropy loss), while very large or very small ratios allow either free motion or exclusion. This mismatch kernel improves MAE of entropy loss/R over baseline.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E05 and E04: shape matching between guest and pore controls adsorption state and mobility; a window function of the size ratio captures the commensurability mechanism of confinement entropy, nonlinearly combining pore aperture and molecular span.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If the fitted response to this descriptor is not peaked near ratio 1 (e.g., partial dependence is monotonic over the observed range) and MAE does not decrease versus baseline, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: surface_packing_index
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R increases with the dimensionless ratio of molecular surface area to the two-thirds power of molecular volume, because high surface-to-size molecules make more wall contacts and lose more translational/rotational freedom in the pore; adding this term on top of the full 14-input network lowers MAE of entropy loss/R versus the round-1 retained baseline (MAE_R 0.5431).
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E01: entropy loss upon adsorption reflects quenched translational/rotational degrees of freedom, which scale with the number of molecule-wall contacts; a surface/volume^(2/3) shape factor is a contact-count proxy distinct from the volumetric confinement ratio (AV/Vol) already retained.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If MAE of (s_gas - s_ads)/R does not decrease relative to 0.5431, or the partial dependence of entropy loss/R on this index is flat or of opposite sign, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: channel_span_elongation
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R grows monotonically with the ratio of the longest channel dimension (max of free-sphere and pore-limiting diameter) to the molecular span: long channel segments with tight spans suppress translation along the channel axis more than cage-like or oversized pores. Including this ratio reduces MAE of entropy loss/R below the round-1 baseline.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E01 (TON vs FAU entropy-loss contrast) and E05 (shape matching in tubular pores): channel dimensionality and guest length jointly determine how many translational modes survive; the ratio couples both largest framework length scales (lsd_f, lsd_p) to molecular elongation (SPAN), information the retained volumetric ratio does not encode.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If MAE of entropy loss/R does not improve below 0.5431, or permutation importance of this descriptor is not significant (p > 0.05), or its partial dependence is non-monotonic in the predicted direction, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: gravimetric_pore_compaction
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Frameworks with high skeleton density relative to accessible pore volume (compact walls, small effective free space per gram) impose stiffer confinement and larger entropy loss/R than porous frameworks at equal molecular size; adding this gravimetric compaction term lowers MAE of entropy loss/R versus the round-1 baseline.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E01/E03: occupiable volume is the single dominant material descriptor, but it conflates pore amount with wall compactness; density (source numerical scale, no unverified units assumed) provides an independent measure of framework mass packing per pore space, separating dense small-pore topologies (e.g., TON-like) from open large-cage ones (e.g., FAU-like).
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If MAE of entropy loss/R does not decrease relative to 0.5431, or the descriptor's partial dependence shows no distinguishable structure (permutation p > 0.05) after accounting for the retained AV/Vol term, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: pore_window_freedom_index
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R is governed jointly by the aperture-restriction contrast (free-sphere vs pore-limiting diameter) and the absolute pore volume per gram: frameworks with a large lsd_f/lsd_p contrast (narrow windows opening into larger free spheres) trap guests in cages and cause larger entropy loss than open channels at equal AV. Adding this coupled re-expression to the full 14-input network lowers MAE of entropy loss/R below the round-1 retained baseline (0.5431).
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E01 (TON largest, FAU smallest entropy loss, i.e., cage/window topology matters beyond occupiable volume alone) and E05 (window-controlled adsorption states): the ratio lsd_f/lsd_p distinguishes cage-like from channel-like topologies, and multiplying by a volume term makes the descriptor vanish for small-pore, low-free-volume frameworks. The retained AV/Vol term encodes only packing tightness, not window geometry, so this adds distinct information.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If MAE of (s_gas - s_ads)/R does not decrease below 0.5431, or permutation importance of this descriptor is insignificant (p > 0.05) after accounting for the retained AV/Vol term, or its partial dependence is inconsistent with a cage-trapping regime, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: molecular_pore_elongation_mismatch
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R increases with the mismatch between molecular elongation (PMI3/PMI1 inertia ratio) and the cube-root size scale (Vol^(1/3)): highly elongated molecules in similarly elongated channels retain one translational mode (moderate loss), while compact molecules lose all modes in tight pores; the deviation from the matched regime, captured by the absolute log-ratio, tracks the excess entropy loss beyond what volumetric confinement explains. Including this descriptor lowers MAE of entropy loss/R below 0.5431.
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E01 (entropy loss decomposes into translational + rotational parts, with framework-dependent residual) and E09 (molecular symmetry controls mobility under confinement): inertia anisotropy measures how many rotational modes can survive, and dividing by a volume-based length scale converts it into a dimensionless shape-vs-size commensurability index distinct from the round-1 rejected symmetric anisotropy (which ignored size) and from the retained volumetric ratio.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If MAE does not improve below 0.5431, or the partial dependence is flat or has the sign opposite to a U-shaped commensurability response, the hypothesis is falsified.

descriptor_candidates.name: gravimetric_surface_confinement
descriptor_candidates.hypothesis: Entropy loss/R grows with the ratio of framework-specific surface area per pore volume (ASA/AV, wall-contact availability) relative to the molecule's own surface-per-volume density (LabuteASA/Vol): frameworks offering many wall sites per unit pore space relative to the guest's contact density immobilize guests more strongly, so adding this material-vs-molecule surface coupling lowers MAE of entropy loss/R below the round-1 retained baseline (0.5431).
descriptor_candidates.rationale: Inference from E01 (entropy loss = quenched translational/rotational freedom, framework-specific) and E03 (occupiable volume is dominant but conflates pore amount with wall abundance): ASA per AV measures wall richness of the framework, while LabuteASA per Vol measures the guest's contact-demandingness; their ratio is a host-guest contact efficiency term not captured by the retained pure volumetric ratio or by either surface term alone.
descriptor_candidates.falsification_criteria: If MAE of (s_gas - s_ads)/R does not decrease relative to 0.5431, or the partial dependence of entropy loss/R on this descriptor is flat or monotonic in the direction opposite to increasing wall-contact efficiency, the hypothesis is falsified.
